finding.claim: HIGH: The unauthenticated public route POST /hooks/test passes the request-body field `callback` directly to axios.post as the full URL. Nothing restricts the host or scheme, so an attacker can make the server send requests to internal services, RFC-1918 addresses or cloud metadata endpoints. axios follows redirects by default, so an allowlist on the initial URL would not have closed this either. The response body is not returned, but the upstream HTTP status code is, which allows internal port and host probing.

trace.note: `pub` router is created separately from `admin`; no auth middleware is attached to it in this file
req.body.callback is used unmodified as the axios.post URL; axios follows redirects by default
r.status is returned to the caller (status oracle). A failed request throws in an async handler with no try/catch, which can give a differential error signal

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, URL parsing, scheme check or hostname check anywhere on the path. The `requireAdmin` middleware (routes.js:7-12) is applied only to the `admin` router via admin.use (routes.js:12), not to `pub`. There is no app or server file in the repo, so any auth applied when mounting `pub` could not be checked; reachability assumes `pub` is mounted without auth. No redirect restriction (maxRedirects is not set). No egress CIDR config in the repo.

verdict.reason: routes.js:20 passes req.body.callback unmodified to axios.post in the `pub` router, which has no auth middleware (requireAdmin is only on `admin` at routes.js:12), no host or scheme validation exists, and routes.js:21 returns the upstream status; the only caveat is that the mount point of `pub` isn't in the repo.

finding.claim: MEDIUM: The admin-only route GET /diagnostics/fetch passes the query parameter `url` directly to axios.get with no allowlist. An authenticated admin can make the server request internal hosts or cloud metadata and see the response status. The route is behind requireAdmin, so it is MEDIUM rather than HIGH. Per the skill, admin-only does not close SSRF to metadata or RFC-1918 targets, and nothing shows that admin implies OS-level access.

trace.note: admin.use(requireAdmin) gates the router on session role === 'admin'
req.query.url is used unmodified as the axios.get URL; axios follows redirects by default
r.status is returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: requireAdmin (routes.js:7-10) checks req.session.role === 'admin', so reaching the sink needs an admin session. That is an authorization barrier but not a URL validation. No allowlist, scheme restriction, redirect restriction or IP-range blocking exists. The session is populated elsewhere (not in the repo), so its integrity could not be verified.

verdict.guard_found: none for URL validation; the router is gated by requireAdmin (routes.js:7-10, applied at routes.js:12), which checks session role === 'admin'
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate, but the url reaching axios.get at routes.js:15 can only be supplied by a session that passes requireAdmin (routes.js:8, 12). That is not an unauthenticated or low-privilege source under the stated criteria, so this is not an attacker-controlled SSRF. The unauthenticated-reachable sink is the separate pub.post('/hooks/test') at routes.js:20, which this finding does not cover.
